identity.method_name: Split (inductive) conformal prediction, jackknife+ and CV+ (Barber, Candes, Ramdas, Tibshirani 2021), and conformalised quantile regression / CQR (Romano, Patterson, Candes 2019)
identity.core_idea: A calibration wrapper placed around any already-trained point-estimate or quantile model. It computes 'conformity scores' (typically absolute residuals, or for CQR, distances beyond predicted quantiles) on a held-out calibration set, takes the appropriate empirical quantile of those scores, and uses it to widen the point prediction into an interval or set. The resulting interval is guaranteed, by a finite-sample exchangeability argument (not an asymptotic or distributional one), to contain the true value of whatever the model was trained to predict with a user-chosen probability (e.g. 90%), on average over exchangeable draws -- it needs no assumption about the model's correctness, the noise distribution, or the sample size beyond a handful of calibration points.
identity.official_dataset_ids: None. This is a general-purpose statistical wrapper, not a dataset; it would be applied to whatever point-estimate model the project builds on its own 42-row lake-year table or its pixel/patch-level derivatives.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Not a labelling strategy in the usual sense -- conformal prediction is orthogonal to the ground-truth problem. It does not create, validate, or substitute for encroachment labels; it calibrates an honest uncertainty band around whatever target the underlying model was already trained to predict, proxy or otherwise. Whatever labelling strategy the base model uses (e.g. the project's own MNDWI/NDVI threshold, or a weak/programmatic label), conformal prediction inherits that target unchanged and says nothing about whether it is correct.
fit_to_project.input_required: A trained point-estimate or quantile-regression base model, plus a calibration set of (features, label) pairs drawn from the SAME label the base model targets, held out from training but assumed exchangeable with future test points. No new data source is required beyond what the base model already needs.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: only-if-reframed, and the reframing is exactly what the jackknife+ and CV+ variants exist for. Classic split conformal requires carving out a dedicated calibration subset (commonly 15-25% of the data) and holding it out from training; at n=42 that means sacrificing roughly 6-11 rows purely for calibration, which is a real cost when the base model is already data-starved. Jackknife+ and CV+ were developed precisely to avoid this: jackknife+ uses n leave-one-out refits so nearly all n=42 rows contribute to both training and calibration, and CV+ does the analogous thing with K folds, at the cost of K (or n) refits of the base model rather than a single fit. The effective independent sample size, however, is still bounded below by the number of distinct lakes (6), not 42, if the target is correlated within a lake across its 7 years -- which is very likely for any encroachment-related quantity, so the true information content behind the calibration guarantee is closer to 6 clusters than 42 rows.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: needs-weak-labels -- more precisely, it needs whatever label (weak, proxy, or otherwise) the wrapped base model already targets. It does not need a NEW or BETTER label than the base model uses; it also cannot upgrade a bad label into a good one. If the base model predicts a proxy quantity (e.g. a MNDWI-based water-loss score), conformal prediction produces a rigorous interval around THAT proxy quantity, not around verified encroachment status.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Not resolution-dependent. Conformal prediction is agnostic to the feature representation of the base model -- it works identically whether the wrapped model operates on 20 m pixel-level features, patch-level CNN outputs, or the 42-row lake-year tabular features. No foreign pretrained-resolution assumption is introduced.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: Whichever label source the wrapped base model already uses; conformal prediction introduces no new label requirement, and correspondingly provides no new label quality.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Most directly addresses limitation (3) (no real ground truth) by converting an undisclosed false-precision point estimate into an explicit, quantified, and honestly-scoped uncertainty statement -- this is the closest thing in the whole project to a genuine fix for the ground-truth problem, though it fixes the DISCLOSURE of the problem, not the problem itself (see viable_without_ground_truth). It also meaningfully mitigates limitation (1) (only 42 rows), since jackknife+ and CV+ exist specifically to make small-n calibration workable without sacrificing a large held-out split. It does not address limitation (2) (OpenStreetMap buildings as a single static snapshot) or limitation (4) (one dry-season scene per year) -- it wraps whatever features and labels those limitations already constrain.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No. Conformal prediction only calibrates uncertainty around whatever the base model's point prediction and label already represent; if the underlying proxy label conflates a drained-for-desilting lake with an encroached one, the conformal interval will be a well-calibrated interval around that CONFLATED, confounded quantity -- honestly quantified but not corrected. It cannot detect or separate the desilting confound on its own.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No, for the same reason. A conformal interval around a vegetation-based proxy that already misclassifies water hyacinth as vegetation will faithfully report how uncertain that (wrong) number is, not correct the underlying spectral confusion. Any fix to the hyacinth confound has to happen in the base model or the label definition, not in the conformal wrapper.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None. Conformal prediction is a purely statistical calibration layer with no inherent connection to any legal or cadastral boundary; it neither improves nor degrades whatever legal traceability (or lack of it) the underlying prediction task already has relative to the OpenStreetMap proxy polygon, the 30 m Master Plan buffer, or the 75 m National Green Tribunal buffer.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: Irrelevant to the mechanics of the method itself -- it does not care whether an input feature varies annually or is a static snapshot. It DOES interact with the exchangeability assumption: because the calibration and test data here are lake-years drawn from a temporally evolving, serially correlated process (each of 6 lakes observed sequentially across 7 years), values are not literally i.i.d. draws, which is the classic exchangeability requirement split conformal relies on (see risk/failure_modes).

implementation.libraries: MAPIE (scikit-learn-contrib, https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/MAPIE) -- provides split conformal, jackknife+, CV+ ('plus' methods) and conformalised quantile regression (CQR) through a scikit-learn-compatible MapieRegressor / MapieClassifier API; alternatives include crepes, puncc, and nonconformist for the same core methods, and a from-scratch numpy implementation is feasible given how small the calibration computation is at this scale.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Not applicable -- conformal prediction wraps whatever base model (a Random Forest, gradient-boosted tree, CNN, or linear model) has already been trained; it introduces no weights of its own.
implementation.licence: MAPIE is BSD-3-Clause licensed (a scikit-learn-contrib project), fully open and usable in an academic project with no restriction.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial for plain split conformal (one calibration pass, negligible cost). Jackknife+ and CV+ require n (or K) refits of the base model -- at n=42 that is 42 refits for jackknife+, which is negligible if the base model is a classical-ML model (Random Forest, gradient boosting, linear/logistic regression) fit in well under a second each, and is still feasible on free Colab/Kaggle GPU time if the base model is a CNN or transformer, though 42 full retrainings of a deep model would meaningfully add to the project's total compute budget and should be planned for rather than assumed free.
implementation.student_days: Roughly 1-3 student-days to wrap an already-trained point-estimate model with MAPIE's split conformal or jackknife+/CV+ methods and produce calibrated intervals with an empirical coverage check, assuming the base model already exists; add about 1 day if conformalised quantile regression is implemented instead (requires a quantile-regression base model, e.g. gradient-boosted quantile trees or a quantile loss neural net, rather than a plain point estimator).

evaluation.metrics: Empirical coverage (the fraction of held-out points whose true -- i.e. proxy-label -- value falls inside the produced interval, compared against the nominal target such as 90%), and average interval width as the efficiency counterpart (a method that trivially achieves 100% coverage by returning an infinitely wide interval is useless, so width must be reported alongside coverage). Per-lake or per-group conditional coverage should also be checked, since marginal coverage over all 42 lake-years can mask systematically poor coverage for a subset of lakes.
evaluation.validation_protocol: Leave-one-lake-out at the outer level, to get an honest estimate of coverage that is not inflated by a lake appearing in both calibration and evaluation; jackknife+ or CV+ is then applied at an inner level, over the remaining lakes' lake-years, to perform the actual conformal calibration without sacrificing a large held-out split. This nested structure is necessary specifically because of the confound between the project's own leakage risk (same lake in train and test) and the conformal method's own internal use of leave-one-out/K-fold refitting for calibration -- the two leave-one-out procedures serve different purposes and must not be conflated into a single, single-level cross-validation.
evaluation.leakage_risk: The dominant, project-specific leakage risk is drawing the calibration and evaluation lake-years from the SAME lake rather than holding out entire lakes: because years within a lake are strongly serially correlated, a within-lake temporal split will look well-calibrated only because the calibration set has effectively memorised that lake's own noise and trend profile, not because the method generalises to lakes it has not seen. This is the same spatial/cluster leakage risk that affects every other item in this project's outline, but here it directly undermines the specific statistical guarantee (marginal exchangeable coverage) that is the entire point of using conformal prediction, so it is especially important to get the split right here.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: This IS the uncertainty-reporting method -- by construction it replaces a bare point estimate with a calibrated interval, which is the strongest possible answer to this field of any item in the outline. The caveat is that the guarantee is marginal (averaged over the calibration/test population) and only as good as the exchangeability assumption holds; jackknife+ and CV+ in particular only guarantee coverage of at least 1-2*alpha (not the full 1-alpha of exact split conformal) under general conditions, so a claimed 90% target (alpha=0.10) technically only guarantees at least 80% worst-case coverage unless additional stability conditions on the base algorithm hold.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable in the direct sense -- none of split conformal, jackknife+, CV+, or CQR synthesise new data points; they only reweight and quantile-transform residuals computed from real, already-observed data. The nearest analogous risk would arise only if a weighted-conformal variant were used to correct for covariate shift by re-weighting the calibration set, which is not part of the plain methods recommended here and would need its own disclosure if introduced later.

evidence.published_performance: Split conformal and full conformal prediction guarantee marginal coverage of exactly 1-alpha under exchangeability by construction (a theoretical, not merely empirical, result: Vovk, Gammerman, Shafer 2005, and restated accessibly in Angelopoulos and Bates, arXiv:2107.07511). Barber, Candes, Ramdas and Tibshirani (2021), 'Predictive inference with the jackknife+', Annals of Statistics, prove a coverage guarantee of at least 1-2*alpha for jackknife+ and CV+ under exchangeability and algorithmic symmetry, weaker than exact split conformal's 1-alpha but requiring no dedicated calibration hold-out. Romano, Patterson and Candes (2019), 'Conformalized Quantile Regression', NeurIPS, report empirical coverage close to the nominal target with materially narrower average interval width than fixed-width split conformal on several UCI benchmark regression datasets [verify exact numeric coverage/width figures against the primary paper before quoting them]. Singh et al. (2024), 'Uncertainty quantification for probabilistic machine learning in Earth observation using conformal prediction', Scientific Reports, doi 10.1038/s41598-024-65954-w (PMC11246475), empirically demonstrate that split conformal methods achieve close-to-nominal marginal coverage across several regression and classification Earth-observation tasks spanning local to global scales, while also documenting that only about 22.5% of surveyed EO datasets report any uncertainty information at all [verify exact percentage and per-task coverage figures against the primary source].
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: Angelopoulos and Bates is a methodological tutorial with illustrative examples (ImageNet classification, medical imaging), not a study of any lake or wetland. Barber et al. 2021 is a theoretical statistics paper with simulation studies, not an applied geospatial study. Romano et al. 2019 uses standard UCI tabular regression benchmarks. Singh et al. 2024 (PMC11246475) is the most relevant precedent: it is explicitly an Earth-observation application, covering multiple EO regression and classification tasks at scales from local to global, but the specific case studies are not lakes, wetlands, or Bengaluru [verify which specific EO tasks/domains are covered in that paper before citing exact application matches].
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No application of conformal prediction to Indian urban lakes, Bengaluru lakes, or lake/wetland encroachment specifically was found. The closest relevant precedent remains Singh et al. 2024 (PMC11246475), which is Earth observation generally but not this domain or geography.
evidence.evidence_recency: Strong and current: Romano, Patterson, Candes 2019 (CQR); Barber, Candes, Ramdas, Tibshirani 2021 (jackknife+/CV+, published in the Annals of Statistics); Angelopoulos and Bates 2021 (arXiv:2107.07511, widely used tutorial, revised through at least v6); Singh et al. 2024 (PMC11246475, Earth-observation-specific application). The only pre-2020 reference is the foundational Vovk, Gammerman, Shafer 2005 conformal prediction book, which falls under the brief's carve-out for core statistical theory.

(2021), 'Predictive inference with the jackknife+', Annals of Statistics 49(1), https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-statistics/volume-49/issue-1/Predictive-inference-with-the-jackknife/10.1214/20-AOS1965.pdf; Romano, Y., Patterson, E., Candes, E.J. (2019), 'Conformalized Quantile Regression', NeurIPS 2019 / arXiv:1905.03222, https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.03222; Singh, G., Moncrieff, G., Venter, Z., Cawse-Nicholson, K., Slingsby, J., Robinson, T.B. (2024), 'Uncertainty quantification for probabilistic machine learning in earth observation using conformal prediction', Scientific Reports 14, doi 10.1038/s41598-024-65954-w, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11246475/; MAPIE documentation and source, https://mapie.readthedocs.io/ and https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/MAPIE ; Cherubin, Nouretdinov, Gammerman et al., 'MAPIE: an open-source library for distribution-free uncertainty quantification', arXiv:2207.12274; Tibshirani, R.J. et al., 'Conformal Prediction Beyond Exchangeability', Annals of Statistics 2023, https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~ryantibs/papers/nexcp.pdf (for the exchangeability-violation discussion).

risk.failure_modes: (1) Exchangeability violated by clustered panel structure: with only 6 lakes observed repeatedly over 7 years, lake-years from the same lake are not exchangeable with lake-years from a different lake (each lake has its own baseline morphology, catchment, and desilting/hyacinth regime) -- if calibration and evaluation lake-years are pooled without respecting the lake grouping, the coverage guarantee is only valid for the pooled, lake-blind population, not for any individual lake, and effectively double- (or seven-times-) counts each lake's own idiosyncratic behaviour across its 7 years as if they were 7 independent draws. (2) With 6 clusters it is essentially impossible to also demonstrate per-lake conditional coverage with any statistical power -- only marginal coverage over the pooled 42 lake-years can be honestly claimed. (3) At n=42, jackknife+/CV+'s theoretical worst-case guarantee is only 1-2*alpha, not 1-alpha, so a nominal 90% target has a proven floor of only 80% in the worst case, which should be disclosed rather than presented as if it were the tighter split-conformal guarantee. (4) Garbage-in-garbage-out: conformal prediction is entirely silent on whether the wrapped point prediction or its label is meaningful, unbiased, or reflective of reality -- a perfectly calibrated 90% interval around a confounded, desilting- and hyacinth-contaminated proxy score is still wrong about the real world 90% of the time it is 'right' about the proxy, just precisely and honestly so.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel is very likely to ask exactly the question posed in the task brief: 'does a 90% conformal interval mean you are 90% confident the lake was actually encroached?' The correct, defensible answer is NO -- conformal prediction gives coverage over the project's OWN DERIVED LABEL (e.g. a MNDWI/NDVI-based proxy score), assuming the calibration and test lake-years are exchangeable; it gives no guarantee whatsoever about the TRUE encroachment state, because no verified ground truth exists to calibrate against in the first place (project_constraints.ground_truth: None). If this distinction is stated explicitly, repeatedly, and in the same sentence as any reported coverage number, this is one of the few genuinely strong, sophisticated, and honest additions available in the whole project, because it directly confronts the panel's most obvious attack ('how do you know that number is real with no ground truth?') instead of avoiding it. If the distinction is glossed over, a claimed '90% confidence interval' will read to a panel as an overstated, misleading claim of validated accuracy the project does not have.
risk.honest_expectation: Realistically achievable: a statistically rigorous (though proxy-label-only) prediction interval around whatever point-estimate encroachment-risk score the project's chosen model produces, built with jackknife+ or CV+ specifically to cope with n=42, and evaluated for empirical coverage using a leave-one-lake-out protocol. Not achievable, and should not be claimed: validity, coverage, or confidence with respect to the TRUE, unobserved encroachment status of any lake. Expect intervals that are wider than hoped once lake-clustering is properly respected in the calibration/evaluation split, and a coverage check that is only approximately -- not exactly -- nominal, given the exchangeability violation from the 6-lake panel structure. This is a modest, honest, well-supported addition, not a solution to the project's ground-truth problem.

verdict.recommended_rank: adopt -- of everything in this project's outline, this is the cheapest, most mechanically simple (given any existing point-estimate model), and most directly targeted at the project's single biggest credibility weakness (false precision with zero ground truth); it should be applied to whichever point-estimate model the project ultimately adopts, using jackknife+ or CV+ given n=42, with the coverage claim scoped explicitly to the project's own proxy label rather than to true encroachment status.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We wrap our chosen point-estimate encroachment-risk model in a jackknife+/CV+ conformal interval (via MAPIE) so we can state, with a proven finite-sample guarantee, that our declared risk band contains our own MNDWI/NDVI-based proxy score roughly 90% of the time -- an honest, mathematically guaranteed statement about our own derived label, explicitly not a claim of 90% confidence about verified real-world illegal encroachment, which we have no ground truth to validate against.
